Subject : Reservoir Fluids Study, Dulang A25, B14 & D26S Well
                Our Ref: MFL 20110028

Several reservoir fluid samples consisting of separator liquid, separator gas, stocktank oil and water samples were collected from Dulang A25, B14 & D26S well and were forwarded to our Kuala Lumpur laboratory for quality checking prior performing further reservoir fluid analysis. 

Core Laboratories Malaysia Sdn. Bhd. appreciates this opportunity to have been of service to PETRONAS Carigali Sdn. Bhd. (PCSB). Should any questions arise concerning the data presented in this report, or if Core Laboratories Malaysia Sdn. Bhd. may be of assistance in any other matter, please do not hesitate to contact us.







Yours sincerely,

Core Laboratories Malaysia Sdn Bhd




Gurdev Gurdial
Manager
Reservoir Fluids Group

Sample Received
Several reservoir fluid samples consisting of separator liquid, separator gas, water and stock tank oil samples collected from Dulang A25, B14 & D26S well, were received in our Kuala Lumpur laboratory for reservoir fluid study.

Surface Sample Validation (Separator Liquid)
The separator liquid samples were heated to a temperature of 200°F prior to any sample removal in order to eliminate any possible wax precipitation. Upon heating, the  water and mud  amounts in the samples were determined as a quality check. The samples were then transferred into Corelab cylinder prior further analysis and the original cylinders were returned to Halliburton. 

Bubble Point Determination (Separator Liquid)
A portion of separator liquid  sample was charged to a high pressure visual PVT cell at reported separator temperature.  Saturation point determination was then performed during which the bubble point pressure was determined. 
For separator liquid sample from Cyl# 819088, the bubble point was observed to be higher than the reported separator pressure. This observation was forwarded to a representative of PETRONAS Carigali Sdn Bhd. After further discussion, no further analysis was required and to proceed with sample disposal.

Surface Sample Validation (Separator Gas)
The separator gas samples were agitated well and allowed to stabilized at a temperature 20°F above the separator temperature. The opening pressure, amount of mud and water and the hydrocarbon composition through dodecanes plus (see below) were then determined from the validation process. The samples were then transferred into Corelab cylinder prior further analysis and the original cylinders were returned to Halliburton. 

Sample Composition by Flash Separation
The composition of the separator liquid sample was determined using a flash separation technique and gas chromatography. The schematic diagram of flash separation technique is presented as Figure 1 on page A.2 of this report. The liquid was flashed at atmospheric pressure and a controlled temperature of 120°F and separated into gas and liquid phases.  The gas was analysed by extended gas analysis technique  and the liquid by temperature programmed  high resolution capillary gas chromatography. Refer Gas Composition and Stablised Liquid Composition (below) for detailed explanation on gas chromatography techniques.  The two analyses were then mathematically recombined to the flash gas-liquid ratio. 

Gas Composition
Gas composition was determined using extended gas chromatography by the GPA 2286 method using a multi-column gas chromatograph system.  A single partial pressure charge is passed through the sampling valve and charged to each analytical column. The TCD (Thermal Conductivity Detector) reads O2, N2 and C1 from the molecular sieve column followed by C2, CO2, C3, iC4, nC4, iC5, nC5 from the porous polymer column. The FID (Flame Ionization Detector) reads up to Cn+ from the capillary column independently.   A temperature programme was used in order to provide optimum detection and resolution of the dodecanes plus components. 

Stabilised Liquid Compositions
Stabilised liquid compositions were determined by temperature high resolution capillary gas chromatography using a cold-on-column injection technique. This injection technique involves the sample being deposited directly onto the front end of a wide bore capillary column. The sample is injected cold (35°C) to eliminate flashback through the injector port. Once the injection is complete, the front end of the column is rapidly heated to 300°C to vapourise the sample. The various constituents of the sample then elute through  the column at different retention times into a Flame Ionisation Detector (FID). The output or signal of the detector is proportional to the amount of a component or constituent present in the sample. Note that the FID response is proportional to the number of the carbon atoms, therefore the FID can be regarded as a mass detector.













Sample Selection
Upon reviewing the validation data, a representative of Talisman Malaysia Ltd.  has selected separator pair 2.01a & 2.01c (Separator Gas from Cyl#  5030 A & Separator Liquid from Cyl# TS 4709 respectively) for wellstream compositions calculation. 
During validation checking, the saturation pressure of the separator liquid sample (Cyl# TS 4709) was observed to be higher than the reported separator pressure at the reported separator temperature. A representative of Talisman Malaysia Ltd has requested Corelab to perform saturation pressure adjustment on this sample to obtain the saturation pressure equal to the separator pressure prior further analysis.

Summary of Analysis Methods (Basic Properties Analyses)

Sample Selection
Two stocktank oil samples were received and selected for Compositional & Basic Properties Analyses. 

Stabilised Liquid Composition
The composition of the stock tank samples were determined by high resolution capillary gas chromatography utilising a cold-on-column injection technique. This injection technique involves the sample being deposited directly onto the front end of a wide bore capillary column. The sample is injected cold (35°C) to eliminate flashback through the injector port. Once the injection is completed, the front end of the column is rapidly heated to 300°C to vapourise the sample. The various constituents of the sample then elute through  the column at different retention times into a Flame Ionisation Detector (FID). The output or signal of the detector is proportional to the amount of the component or constituent present in the sample. Note that the FID response is proportional to the number of the carbon atoms, therefore the FID can be regarded as a mass detector.The composition and liquid chromatogram of stock tank sample are presented in Section C.

Basic Crude Properties Analyses
A series of Basic Crude Properties analyses, i.e. Density, Pour Point, Paraffin Wax Content & Water Content Tests were performed on the selected sample. These analyses were performed in accordance to American Society for Testing and Materials (ASTM), The Institute of Petroleum (IP) and Universal Oil Product Company (UOP) test methods. 

Wax Appearance Temperature 
The Wax Appearance Temperature was determined by Differential Scanning Calorimetry (DSC). DSC measures the heat of crystallization of formation of wax crystal in the oil sample during the cooling cycle. The point (temperature) at which the heat of crystallization is detected is considered to be Wax Appearance Temperature. The cooling rate used for the measurement was 10°C/minute respectively.

Summary of Analysis Methods (Water Analyses)

Sample Received

Two water samples were received and selected for API 12 ion Water Analysis, Resistivity, pH, Specific Gravity, Total Dissolved Solids and Scaling Potential analyses.  

Water Compositional Analysis

Elemental Analysis – The sample was filtered through a Whatman No. 5 filter paper and a dilution made, using distilled water, according to their salinity. This is to ensure that all the elements are in the correct range for ICP analysis.  The result is presented in mg/l on the ICP (Inductively Coupled Plasma Atomic Emission Spectroscopy) for all detectable elements found in formation waters, seawaters and drilling fluids. A routine water analysis consists of determining the following ions by ICP technique – sodium, potassium, calcium, magnesium, barium, strontium, dissolved iron, sulphate (as total sulphur), phosphorus, silicon, boron, aluminium and lithium.

Chloride – The diluted sample was then analysed for chloride content by titration with silver nitrate solution using an ion selective electrode. Before use, the instrument was calibrated by running a quality control sample.

pH / Bicarbonate / Carbonate – pH and bicarbonate determinations were measured by ion selective electrode. The instrument was first calibrated using pH 10, 7 and 4 buffers and checked using a bicarbonate quality control sample. The pH and bicarbonate determinations were performed on filtered undiluted sample. The pH of a sample was initially determined using an ion selective electrode.  If pH is above 8.1, the sample is titrated with sulphuric acid for carbonate down to pH 8.1 then down to pH 4.1 for bicarbonate.

Total Iron – The measurement was performed on unfiltered & undiluted sample.  A 10ml aliquot of water was sub-sampled and heated on a hotplate after the addition of hydrochloric acid.  The sample was filtered into a 100 ml flask and made up to the mark with distilled water (x 10 dilution). The sample was then read on the ICP for total iron concentration.

Specific Gravity & Density – This was determined by Densitymeter on a filtered & undiluted sample. The temperature was set at 15.6°C and the specific gravity is reported at 60°F. 

Resistivity – The  resistivity was performed on filtered & undiluted sample using a null point method and noting the temperature.  The resistivity is reported as a calculated value at 60°F.

Further Analysis
Further PVT study was not required for these samples as informed by a representative of PETRONAS Carigali Sdn Bhd. These samples were requested to be disposed.
